questions.topic: Range of a projectile over level ground
questions.learningObjective: Explain why range depends on launch angle and speed
questions.stem: Why does a projectile's range over level ground increase with launch speed but not always with launch angle?

answer.exemplar: Range grows with the square of launch speed because both time of flight and horizontal speed increase. For a fixed speed, range peaks near 45 degrees and falls toward 0 or 90 degrees because a steeper angle shortens horizontal speed while a shallower angle shortens air time.

questions.explanation: The range formula combines horizontal speed and time of flight, so speed squared scales range. Angle trades off horizontal speed against air time, giving a maximum near 45 degrees.
questions.hint: Think about horizontal speed and air time together.

questions.learningObjective: Compute range from speed and angle
questions.stem: What two quantities determine the range of a projectile launched over level ground?

answer.exemplar: Launch speed and launch angle determine the range through v squared sin 2theta over g. Speed enters squared, while angle enters through sin 2theta, which peaks at 45 degrees.

questions.explanation: The range formula uses v squared and sin 2theta. Thus both speed and angle matter, with speed having a squared effect.

questions.explanation: Range scales with sin 2theta, which peaks at 1 for theta = 45 degrees. Thus 45 degrees gives the greatest range.

questions.explanation: Extra height lengthens flight time, and range equals horizontal speed times that time. Thus range increases.

questions.stem: If a nurse drops a heavy vial and a light vial from the same height, which lands first and why?

answer.exemplar: They land at the same time in the absence of air resistance because fall time depends only on height and g, not mass. Any difference in real life comes from air resistance, not from weight.

questions.explanation: Galileo's result says all objects fall with the same acceleration g when air resistance is negligible. Mass cancels in the kinematic equation.
